title: Measure It
context: Grade 3, the first working topic of the metric measures chapter. An adult sees a ruler held against a pencil, which a real ruler does well. What is being settled is why a fixed unit is needed at all, and how big each unit feels: a centimetre for a clip, a metre for a rope, a kilometre for a road. A child who has never seen two handspans disagree thinks the desk has two lengths, and a child with no feel for the units will write the height of a door in kilometres without a worry.

writeup.why: See that a handspan is not fair and a fixed unit is, choose centimetres, metres or kilometres for a real thing, read a length at a mark on a ruler or a tape that starts at 0, and tell a thing longer than a metre from one shorter, with half a metre and a quarter of a metre.
writeup.look: A workbench with real things on it, a ruler, a tape and a metre rod beside them, three unit bins with benchmark chips, a My list board, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Measure It' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many things have been measured or sorted so far. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A workbench fills the working area, a pale wooden surface drawn flat with every real thing in its natural colours. On the first phase a desk 880 long and 90 deep lies at x 100, y 330. Under it a small handspan strip 80 long at x 100, y 450 and a bigger handspan strip 110 long at x 100, y 500 wait to be laid along the desk, and each takes a count tag in deep blue once laid. On the second phase a shelf of real things runs across the top at x 90, y 214, 980 by 110, holding a paper clip, a rope across a playground, a bus on a road, a classroom wall and a train, each on a card 180 by 100. Three bins stand below at y 430, 280 wide each, at x 100, x 420 and x 740, labelled cm, m and km. Above each bin a benchmark chip 250 by 50 says about: a finger is about 1 cm, a door handle is about 1 m from the floor, about a quarter of an hour of travel is about 1 km. The unit facts 1 m = 100 cm and 1 km = 1000 m sit in a vermilion ring at x 100, y 610, labelled Unit fact. On the third phase a ruler 900 long at x 100, y 330 starts at 0 with sixteen marks evenly spaced and labelled in cm, each 56 apart, and a measuring tape 980 long at x 90, y 470 starts at 0 with a mark every 10 cm. A paper clip, a pencil, a ribbon or a shelf is dragged along them from the zero mark and shown in natural colours. The reading the child types lands in a deep blue tag labelled Given, and a confirmed length lands in a green tag labelled Answer. On the fourth phase the metre rod stands at x 140, y 230, 400 tall, in ten equal tens marked in near-black, from a floor line to the height of a door handle on a classroom door 520 tall at x 260, y 110. Two bins stand at x 560 and x 820, y 360, 240 by 230, labelled longer than the rod and shorter than the rod. The Fold button at x 140, y 650, 150 by 60 folds the rod in half and then in half again, each fold drawing the rod shorter and labelling it half a metre and a quarter of a metre. A My list board 440 by 120 at x 640, y 100 holds four things in each bin. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing a reading or a count into the answer slot, with the keys cm, m and km for the unit. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate, labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag, labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from sit inside a vermilion ring, labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag, labelled Second or Left. Every ruler mark, scale mark and plain edge is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a measure is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The bench shows the last thing measured with its length and its unit in a deep blue tag, beside the metre rod and the ruler that measured it.

phases.win: the two counts light up side by side, then both strips fade and the ruler shows one length for everyone
phases.does: lays each strip along the desk, reads the two different counts, then lays the ruler along the desk and reads the one length
phases.goal: a handspan changes from person to person, so it gives different counts, and a fixed unit gives one answer for everyone
phases.says: Measure the desk with one strip, then with the other. Are the counts the same?
phases.check: Away from the screen: two friends measure the same table with their own footspans. One counts more than the other. Who counted wrongly?
phases.feels: two honest counts for one desk, and then one ruler making them agree
phases.hands: Let two children measure the same desk with their own handspans and say their counts aloud, then measure it with a ruler and say the length together.
phases.tries: First rung: look at the two strips side by side. Second rung: count how many times each strip lies along the desk. Third rung: the same desk with only the ruler, before the strips return.

wrong.why: two counts are two numbers, so it feels as if there were two lengths
wrong.move: says the desk has two different lengths
wrong.screen: the desk stays one desk in the middle of the bench, each strip's count lights up beside the strip that made it, and the ruler laid along the desk gives one length that both strips agree on

wrong.why: a smaller count seems to be a smaller number of mistakes
wrong.move: says the bigger strip counted wrongly
wrong.screen: the two strips are laid side by side on the bench and the bigger strip is seen to cover more of the desk with each lay, so fewer lays are needed

phases.screen: a desk with a small handspan strip and a bigger handspan strip beside it, and a ruler waiting under the bench
phases.soWhat: a handspan changes from person to person, so we use fixed units that are the same for everyone
phases.concept: Hands and feet are not fair: we need fixed units

phases.win: the thing settles in its bin and a mark on the bin counts how many things fit that unit
phases.does: drags each real thing into the bin whose unit fits it, reading the benchmark chips for help
phases.goal: centimetres fit short things, metres fit longer things and kilometres fit far places
phases.says: Which unit fits this thing? Drag it into a bin.
phases.check: Away from the screen: pick three things in the room and say which unit fits each, and one thing that no unit of the three could measure well.
phases.feels: each thing finding a bin where its number is easy to say
phases.hands: Hold a pencil, stand beside a door and point down a road, and say out loud which of centimetres, metres or kilometres each one needs.
phases.tries: First rung: read the three benchmark chips aloud. Second rung: stand the thing beside the metre rod and ask if it is shorter than a rod or longer. Third rung: the same task with only two bins, cm and m, before km returns.

wrong.why: a playground feels very big to a child, so the biggest unit seems to fit
wrong.move: puts the rope across the playground in the km bin
wrong.screen: the benchmark chip above the km bin lights, saying about a quarter of an hour of travel, and the rope is stood beside the road to show it is much shorter

wrong.why: a metre is the unit a child hears first, so it feels like the unit for everything
wrong.move: puts the paper clip in the m bin
wrong.screen: the benchmark chip above the cm bin lights, saying a finger is about 1 cm, and the paper clip is laid beside a finger to show they are alike

phases.screen: a row of real things on the bench with three bins below, cm, m and km, and a benchmark chip above each
phases.soWhat: centimetres fit short things, metres fit longer things and kilometres fit far places

phases.win: the centimetre marks light one by one up to the end of the thing and the length lands in a deep blue tag
phases.does: lays a thing along the ruler or the tape from the zero mark, reads the number at its other end and types it
phases.goal: to measure, put one end of the thing at 0 and read the number at its other end, taken at a mark
phases.says: Put one end at zero. Read the number at the other end.
phases.check: Away from the screen: lay a pencil along a ruler with its end at the 3 mark instead of 0. Why is the last number not the length?
phases.feels: the marks lighting one by one from the edge of the ruler to the end of the thing
phases.hands: Lay a pencil along a paper ruler from the zero mark, read the number at the other end, and then start again with the pencil at the 2 mark to see what goes wrong.
phases.tries: First rung: slide the thing back so one end sits on the zero mark. Second rung: count the marks aloud from 0. Third rung: the same task with a thing that is only a few centimetres long, before the longer things return.

wrong.why: the first mark a child sees is the one, so counting seems to start there
wrong.screen: the zero mark is lit at the edge of the ruler and the thing is slid back to it, and the marks are counted aloud from 0

wrong.why: the last number looks like the length, whatever the starting mark
wrong.move: reads the number at the end of the thing when it does not start at 0
wrong.screen: a second ruler tag shows the starting mark in deep blue and the ending mark in deep blue, and the marks between them are counted in amber, labelled Left

phases.screen: a ruler that starts at 0 and a measuring tape lying across the bench, and a paper clip, a pencil, a ribbon and a shelf waiting
phases.soWhat: to measure, put one end of the thing at 0 and read the number at the other end
phases.concept: Measuring with a ruler and a tape

phases.win: the rod folds in half and in half again, and each folded rod is labelled half a metre and a quarter of a metre
phases.does: drags real things into longer than the rod or shorter than the rod, then folds the rod in half and in half again
phases.goal: a thing is longer than one metre if it goes past the top of the metre rod, and half a metre and a quarter of a metre are the rod folded
phases.says: Is it longer or shorter than the metre rod? Put it in a bin.
phases.check: Away from the screen: fold a strip of paper in half and again. How many equal parts does the strip have, and what fraction of the whole is one part?
phases.feels: the metre rod bending in the middle and each fold making a shorter piece
phases.hands: Stand a one metre rod or a strip of card beside a door, fold it once and then again, and see which things in the room are longer or shorter than each piece.
phases.tries: First rung: stand the thing beside the rod from the floor line. Second rung: look at the top of the rod and ask if the thing goes past it. Third rung: the same task with only very short and very long things, before the close ones return.

wrong.why: a thin thing looks small, so it feels short
wrong.move: puts a long thin thing in shorter than the rod because it is thin
wrong.screen: the thing is stood beside the rod from the same floor line and its top is carried across to the rod, so the length is seen past the top of the rod

wrong.why: the second fold is also a fold in half, so it feels like the same fold
wrong.move: calls the rod folded twice half a metre
wrong.screen: the first fold is labelled half a metre and the second fold is labelled a quarter of a metre, and the two folded rods are laid side by side

phases.screen: the metre rod standing from the floor to a door handle beside a classroom door, two empty bins, and a Fold button
phases.soWhat: a thing is longer than a metre if it goes past the top of the rod, and a quarter of a metre is half of half
phases.concept: Longer or shorter than one metre

writeup.delight: On the first phase, when the ruler is laid along the desk, the two handspan strips slide off to the side, and both counts fade into one length on the ruler. On the fourth phase, when the Fold button is pressed, the metre rod bends in the middle and folds over itself with a small click, then folds again, and the folded pieces take their labels.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a wooden desk lies across the bench with a small handspan strip and a bigger handspan strip beside it, both counts blank, and the ruler waiting under the bench. On the second phase a row of real things sits on the bench, a paper clip, a rope across a playground, a bus on a road, a classroom wall and a train, with the three bins cm, m and km empty below and a benchmark chip above each. On the third the ruler that starts at 0 and the tape lie across the bench with a paper clip, a pencil, a ribbon and a shelf waiting beside them. On the fourth the metre rod stands from the floor to a door handle beside a classroom door, with two empty bins and the Fold button lit. One thing moves, once: the first handspan strip, the first thing on the bench, the zero mark of the ruler or the top of the metre rod gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any real thing on the bench measured with a strip, the ruler, the tape or the metre rod, sorted into the unit bins, and the My list board filled as you like. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on why a handspan is not fair, choosing a unit, reading a ruler or a tape from 0, and longer or shorter than a metre, each on a real thing.

observations.why: a handspan is a different size for different hands, but a centimetre is always the same.
observations.soWhat: a fixed unit gives the same answer for everyone.
observations.observe: The small strip and the bigger strip gave two different counts for one desk, and the ruler gave one length.

observations.why: a unit that is much too small or much too big gives a number that is hard to say.
observations.soWhat: centimetres fit short things, metres fit longer things and kilometres fit far places.
observations.observe: The rope across the playground sat in the m bin and the paper clip in the cm bin.

observations.why: the zero mark is where counting starts, so the last mark is the length.
observations.soWhat: to measure, put one end of the thing at 0 and read the number at the other end.
observations.observe: The ribbon began at the zero mark and its far end lit the number to type.

observations.why: each fold cuts the length of the rod in two equal parts.
observations.soWhat: half a metre is half of the rod and a quarter of a metre is half of that.
observations.observe: The metre rod folded in half and again, and the second fold was shorter than the first.

source_tool.description: A workbench fills the working area, drawn flat in natural colours. On the first phase a desk lies across it with two handspan strips beside it, one small and one bigger; laying each strip along the desk gives two different counts, and then a ruler is laid along it and both counts become one length. On the second phase a row of real things waits on the bench, a paper clip, a rope across a playground, a bus on a road, a classroom wall and a train, with three bins below, cm, m and km. Above each bin sits a benchmark chip that always says about: a finger is about 1 cm, a door handle is about 1 m from the floor, and about a quarter of an hour of travel is about 1 km. The unit facts 1 m = 100 cm and 1 km = 1000 m are written between the bins. On the third phase a ruler that starts at 0, with its marks evenly spaced, and a measuring tape lie across the bench, and a paper clip, a pencil, a ribbon or a shelf is laid along them from the zero mark; the child types the number at the other end, which is always at a mark. On the fourth phase the metre rod stands from the floor to a door handle beside a classroom door, and real things are dragged into two bins, longer than the rod and shorter than the rod; a Fold button folds the rod in half for half a metre and again for a quarter of a metre. A My list board takes four things in each bin for the child's own list. A number pad types a reading or a count. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many things have been measured or sorted.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a ruler, a measuring tape, a metre rod, a paper clip, a pencil, a book, a door, a ribbon, mangoes, a loaf of bread, potatoes, a bag of salt, a two pan balance with iron weights, a kitchen scale, measuring jugs, a glass, a teacup, a bucket, a bottle, a pot, a juice packet. The object is the thing the child measures, weighs or pours, and a plain bar or tank appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every scale is drawn with its marks evenly spaced and its zero at the edge: a ruler from 0, a metre rod in ten equal tens, a jug in equal marks, a balance with its beam level or tilted by the true difference. A reading is always taken at a mark, never between two.

Every unit is written next to its number, and a number is never written bare where a unit belongs. A unit fact is shown with both its sides, so 1 m = 100 cm is one object and one hundred centimetre marks side by side.

Converting is something the child does: a metre rod breaks into a hundred centimetre marks, a kilogram bag pours out a thousand gram dots, a litre jug empties into a thousand millilitre drops. The vermilion ring carries the times 100 or times 1000 step while it happens.
A sum or a difference is laid out in columns, units over their column, the second amount directly under the first, with a carried amount shown above the column it joins.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance. Large amounts are shown as a few tens, hundreds or thousands.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a mark or a reading the child is looking at, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a mango stays yellow and a metal weight stays dark grey. The four roles of the chapter are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate and is labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag and is labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from, such as one metre is one hundred centimetres, sit inside a vermilion ring and are labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag and are labelled Second or Left. Those four are the same four in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Every ruler mark, scale mark, outline and plain edge is near-black, and the stage still reads with the colour taken away because each role is named in writing first.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Start again at zero and count the marks one by one.
voice.onNext: A new thing. Look at how long it is before you choose.
voice.opening: A workbench with a desk, a ruler and a metre rod.
voice.onFinish: You chose the unit and measured from zero every time.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Measure, sort and fold the rod as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Hands and feet are not fair: we need fixed units
Measuring with a ruler and a tape
Longer or shorter than one metre

placement.where: After the class has measured a desk with their own handspans and counted different numbers, and before any unit is named on the board. The tool is what lets two different handspan strips measure the same desk at once and then be replaced by one ruler, and what folds a metre rod in half twice without a paper strip tearing.

answer_key.rule: A handspan or a foot changes from person to person, so it gives different counts for the same thing, and a fixed unit gives the same answer for everyone. Centimetres measure short things, metres measure longer things and kilometres measure far places. One metre is 100 cm and one kilometre is 1000 m. A centimetre is about the width of a finger, a metre is about the height of a door handle from the floor and a kilometre is about a quarter of an hour of travel, always about. To read a ruler, put one end of the thing at 0 and read the number at its other end. A thing is longer than a metre if it goes past the top of the metre rod and shorter if it stops before. Half a metre is half of the rod and a quarter of a metre is half of that.
answer_key.wrong: The thing is laid along the ruler again from 0 with each centimetre mark lighting in turn and counted aloud, or stood beside the metre rod from the same floor line so that the two can be compared. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The desk is the same desk both times.
A bigger handspan covers more of the desk, so fewer handspans are needed.
A handspan changes from person to person, so it is not a fair unit.
A ruler's centimetres are the same for everyone, so a ruler gives one answer.
items.answer: Their handspans are different sizes. A ruler gives the same answer for everyone.
items.question: Two children measure the same desk with their own handspans. One counts 8 handspans and the other counts 6. Why are the counts different?
items.checkpoint: A fixed unit gives the same answer for everyone.
items.misconception: Thinking one child counted wrongly, when both counted right with hands of different sizes.

steps: The rope is much longer than a ruler.
It is much shorter than the road between two towns.
Metres fit longer things, like a rope across a playground.
A centimetre is too small and a kilometre is too big.
items.question: A rope stretches across the school playground. Which unit fits its length best: cm, m or km?
items.checkpoint: Centimetres fit short things, metres fit longer things and kilometres fit far places.
items.misconception: Choosing km because a playground feels big to a child.

steps: Check that one end of the ribbon is at 0.
Read the number at the other end of the ribbon. It is 9.
The ruler counts in centimetres, so the ribbon is 9 cm long.
items.question: A ribbon lies along a ruler. One end is at the 0 mark and the other end is at the 9 mark. How long is the ribbon?
items.checkpoint: Put one end at 0, then read the number at the other end.
items.misconception: Counting the marks from the 1 mark and so giving a length one too short or one too long.

steps: The metre rod reaches about to the door handle.
The door goes up past its handle, so it goes up past the top of the rod.
So the door is longer than one metre.
A pencil does not reach the top of the rod, so it is shorter than one metre.
items.answer: The door is longer than one metre. The pencil is shorter than one metre.
items.question: The metre rod stands from the floor to a door handle. A classroom door goes up higher than its handle. Is the door longer or shorter than one metre? What about a pencil?
items.checkpoint: Stand the thing beside the metre rod from the same floor line and compare.
items.misconception: Judging by how thick or how heavy a thing is instead of how long it is.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Two children measure the same door with their footspans. One counts 9 and the other counts 7. Is the door two different lengths?
items.final_answer: No. The door is one length. Their feet are different sizes, so the counts are different

items.question: A bus drives from one town to the next town. Which unit fits the distance: cm, m or km?
items.final_answer: km, because the towns are far apart

items.question: A tape is laid along a shelf from the 0 mark. The shelf ends at the 87 mark. How long is the shelf?
Is a railway train longer or shorter than one metre?
A tailor measures a cloth with a ruler. A child measures the same cloth with a handspan. Whose measure would give the same answer for any person who measures?
items.final_answer: The ruler's. Centimetres are fixed units, the same for everyone, but a handspan changes with the hand

items.question: A child measures the long wall of a classroom and writes its length in kilometres. Which unit should the child use instead? Why?
items.final_answer: Metres, because a classroom wall is much longer than a ruler and much shorter than a road between towns

items.question: A pencil is laid on a ruler. One end is at the 2 mark, not at 0, and the other end is at the 9 mark. How long is the pencil?
items.final_answer: 7 cm, because the pencil covers the marks from 2 to 9

items.question: A metre rod is folded in half, and then folded in half again. A ribbon is as long as the folded rod. What fraction of a metre is the ribbon? Is it longer or shorter than half a metre?
items.final_answer: A quarter of a metre. It is shorter than half a metre

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: a small strip and a bigger strip are laid along the desk and counted, and each count lights up
starts at 0 and takes a paper clip, a pencil or a ribbon laid along it from the zero mark
takes a longer thing, such as a shelf, laid along it from the zero mark
take a real thing dragged into cm, m or km, with a benchmark chip above each bin
stands from the floor to a door handle so a thing can be compared with it
folds the metre rod in half for half a metre and again for a quarter of a metre
holds four things longer than the rod and four things shorter, chosen by the child
types a reading or a count

teaching_notes: Let two children measure the same desk with their own handspans before the tool opens, and let them argue about it before anyone says why. Then measure it with one ruler and let them see the same answer. Say about every time a benchmark is used: a finger is about a centimetre and a door handle is about a metre, never exactly. Keep to unmistakable things when sorting against the metre rod, and do not ask for the exact length of a benchmark thing. If a child counts a ruler from the 1 mark, ask where the thing starts. If a child writes the height of a door in kilometres, ask which would be a sensible road. Use fresh things: the exercise's own objects are the child's to find.
generation_prompt: Build a length tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, a workbench with real things drawn as recognisable flat illustrations in their natural colours. On the first phase a wooden desk lies across the working area with a small handspan strip and a bigger handspan strip beside it; each strip is laid along the desk and counted, and then a ruler measures it once. On the second phase a row of real things sits on the bench, a paper clip, a rope across a playground, a bus on a road, a classroom wall and a train, with three bins below, cm, m and km, and a benchmark chip above each that says about: a finger, a door handle, a quarter of an hour of travel. On the third phase a 15 cm ruler that starts at 0 with evenly spaced near-black marks and a measuring tape lie across the bench, and a paper clip, a pencil, a ribbon or a shelf is laid along them from the zero mark and read at a mark. On the fourth phase a metre rod stands from the floor to a door handle beside a classroom door, real things are dragged into two bins, longer than the rod and shorter than the rod, and a Fold button folds the rod in half and in half again. A My list board holds the child's four things in each bin. A number pad types a reading. The deep blue tag holds a given reading and the green tag an answer. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the things measured or sorted. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Measure the desk with a handspan strip. Put a thing in the bin that fits its unit. Lay a thing on the ruler from 0. Compare things with the metre rod.
